title: Trump Prepares for Midterm Fallout, Saying He’ll Take the Blame if Republicans Lose
snippet: At a rally in Tennessee, President Donald Trump acknowledged the tough political landscape facing Republicans, predicting he will face the fallout if the GOP loses Congress in the upcoming midterms.
content:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — Heading into a high-stakes midterm election season, President Donald Trump is taking his message directly to the Republican base while bracing for potential political fallout should the GOP lose its majorities in Congress.

Speaking at a packed rally in Tennessee on Saturday, Trump acknowledged the historic headwinds facing the party in power during midterm cycles, predicting that any potential losses will be laid squarely at his feet.

“If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump told the crowd. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any. But I’m working my ass off. You better get out there and vote.”

Rallying the Base in Deep-Red Territory

While midterm elections traditionally penalize the sitting president's party, Trump is relying on a strategy focused heavily on base turnout. Polling averages show Trump’s overall approval rating sitting at 38%, with 59% disapproving, according to NBC News data. However, his support among core loyalists remains formidable.

His appearance in northern Tennessee—a conservative stronghold he carried comfortably in 2024—was aimed at ensuring Republicans do not grow complacent. Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., noted that energizing the grass roots is critical in off-year elections. “It rallies the base,” Burchett said before the event. “And that’s really what we’ve got to see in a midterm election.”

To incentivize voters, Trump dangled an ambitious proposal, repeating a pledge to deliver $5,000 direct payments to adults if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate—a proposal estimated to carry a $1.3 trillion price tag.

Defying Polls and Pushing the Schedule

Throughout his hour-and-a-half speech, Trump forcefully rejected the idea that his standing among voters has faltered. Addressing supporters onstage, he played media clips demonstrating his near-unanimous approval among his core constituency and dismissed negative polling as a “false narrative.”

“I’m very popular, I really am,” Trump insisted to cheers from the arena.

The Tennessee stop capped a relentless campaign push, marking his seventh state visit since the start of October. A scheduled follow-up trip to Alabama was ultimately canceled as Hurricane Isaias approached the southeastern coast.

Beyond campaigning, Trump spent time touting economic metrics from his term, pointing to gains in median household income and reductions in poverty rates. Closing his speech with typical flair, he mused aloud about renaming major natural landmarks, playfully suggesting names like “Trump Ocean” or “Ocean of the Americas.”
